-its a decent schmup.
-vets of the genre will really get a kick out of it.
-casual gamers will enjoy the first 5/6ths of the campaign (the difficulty ramps up exponentially from there)  - honestly, we're lucky we can play it at all the way these games go. 
-no UWHD support (literally need to change monitor settings or game won't run correctly).
-often freezes when minimized with alt-tab. (nit-picky but important but to me)
-one save slot (and no overwrite warning - so beware).
-myriad of difficulty settings but only one is really suitable for casual gamers and only partially (see above). 
-no way to turn down the music without turning down the general volume (SFX necessary for gameplay).
-isn't really worth more than $5 imho (i paid less than $1 and that seems appropriate for how much i'll be able to get out of it as a casual schmup-player) unless you're a true vet of genre.
-ship variety is amazing - the weapons/maneuverability/aesthetic of each really set them apart from one another.
-the campaign narrative is simply but well-executed with beautiful pixel art
-no way (for me at least) to take  F12(STEAM) screenshots (i've noticed this with a few pixel games) and that REALLY sucks because the game can be truly beautiful at points
-final level is much more difficult then the level directly preceding it - but its a doable challenge
-final boss is easily 10x as difficult as the penultimate level directly preceding it. i feel soft-locked from the ending and discouraged from attempting it many more times (tried at least a dozen times to no avail despite being able to complete every other level in 2 attempts or less). some folks will love this sort of challenge - others will loathe it. for me, such intense difficulty progression (especially when it did not exist before) breaks immersion, corrodes fun and general replayability, and seems a peculiar choice for the "casual" difficulty setting of a game (god only knows how bad it is for every other difficulty setting).

Super Galaxy Squadron EX Turbo is a fast-paced vertical shoot ’em up developed by Synset and published by New Blood Interactive that confidently embraces classic arcade design while layering in modern systems that make it welcoming without sacrificing intensity. It is clearly built as a love letter to the golden age of space shooters, but it avoids feeling dated by offering a wide range of customization, difficulty options, and gameplay modes that encourage experimentation and long-term mastery. From the moment the screen fills with enemy fire and pixel explosions, the game establishes itself as a pure, mechanics-driven experience that prioritizes responsiveness and momentum.

The core structure follows traditional vertical scrolling stages where players pilot a starfighter through dense waves of enemies and screen-dominating bosses. The controls are tight and immediately responsive, which is essential given how quickly the action escalates. Enemy patterns are aggressive but readable, allowing skilled players to weave through projectiles rather than relying purely on brute force. Each of the six main stages is carefully paced, gradually introducing more complex enemy formations and hazards that test situational awareness and reflexes without feeling unfair.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its large roster of playable ships. With numerous vessels available, each featuring unique weapons, firing patterns, and defensive traits, the experience changes significantly depending on the chosen craft. Some ships emphasize raw damage output, while others favor mobility, defensive play, or crowd control. This variety transforms replayability, as mastering one ship does not automatically translate to mastery of another. Experimentation is encouraged, and players can tailor their approach to suit their personal preferences or the demands of higher difficulty settings.

Super Galaxy Squadron EX Turbo also offers several gameplay modes that expand its appeal beyond a single arcade run. The standard arcade mode delivers a classic progression through the main stages, while endless mode shifts the focus toward endurance and score chasing as waves become increasingly relentless. Boss rush mode isolates the game’s most intense encounters, offering a concentrated test of skill and pattern recognition. These modes give players multiple ways to engage with the same core mechanics, extending the game’s lifespan and keeping the experience fresh.

A standout feature that distinguishes the game from more traditional shooters is its use of focus-based mechanics that allow players to briefly slow down the action. This system provides a crucial safety valve during overwhelming moments, giving players time to react, reposition, and make deliberate decisions amid chaos. Combined with overdrive-style power boosts that amplify firepower and scoring potential, these mechanics create a satisfying risk-and-reward loop. Skilled players can push themselves aggressively for higher scores, while newer players can use these tools as a learning aid without feeling overwhelmed.

Visually, the game adopts a clean and colorful pixel art style that prioritizes clarity above all else. Enemy projectiles, ship sprites, and environmental effects are easy to distinguish, even during the most chaotic encounters. While the aesthetic does not aim for high-detail realism, it succeeds in evoking classic arcade shooters while remaining visually readable on modern displays. Explosions and particle effects add a sense of impact, reinforcing the power of weapons and the intensity of boss battles.

The audio design complements the on-screen action with energetic music and punchy sound effects that help maintain momentum. The soundtrack drives the pace of each stage, while weapon and explosion sounds provide satisfying feedback that reinforces player actions. Narrative elements are minimal, offering just enough framing to contextualize the battles without distracting from the gameplay. This restraint suits the genre, keeping the focus squarely on mechanics and performance.

Difficulty is handled with notable flexibility. While the game can become brutally challenging on higher settings, it also includes more forgiving options that allow players to ease into the genre. Health systems, adjustable difficulty, and supportive mechanics help bridge the gap between casual players and genre veterans. The challenge curve feels deliberate, encouraging improvement rather than punishing mistakes excessively, which is a balance many arcade-inspired games struggle to achieve.

Ultimately, Super Galaxy Squadron EX Turbo succeeds because it understands what makes shoot ’em ups compelling. It delivers intense, skill-driven gameplay supported by thoughtful systems that reward practice and experimentation. While its stage count is modest, the variety of ships, modes, and difficulty options ensures that the experience remains engaging over time. For fans of classic vertical shooters or players looking to explore the genre through a polished and accessible entry, it stands as a confident and enjoyable example of modern shmup design rooted firmly in arcade tradition.

Un Shoot'em up simple y bueno de la línea danmaku (te tiran muchas balas, pero tienes hurtbox pequeña y tiras también muchas balas). No destaca especialmente en nada pero da lo que promete y te deja a gusto.
He tardado un poco mas de 13hs de juego neto en completar el 100% y ha estado entretenido la verdad.

[h3]Cosas Positivas[/h3]

- [u][b]Variedad de Naves[/b][/u]: el juego cuenta con 17 naves. Sin embargo se podría decir fácilmente que unas 7 u 8 de esas naves son olvidables, malas, o simplemente no se diferencian lo suficiente de las demás como para justificar su existencia... pero lo bueno es que tienes otras 8 o 9 que están relativamente interesantes con sus mecánicas propias y validez como para que elijas cómo quieres jugar. Mis Favoritas: Green, Black, White y Chrome.

- [u][b]Modos de juego[/b][/u]: Hay tres modos principales. El arcade clásico de toda la vida que puedes jugar en "normal" (donde de pueden dropear vida y puedes continuar todo lo que quieras), o hardcore (donde no te dropean vida y no se puede continuar). El modo Boss Rush que su nombre indica de qué va. Y el modo Endless que es un survival de hacer oleadas tras oleadas hasta ver dónde aguantas. Todo esto cruzado con distintos niveles de dificultad para que lo ajustes a tu disfrute.

- [u][b]Visuals[/b][/u]: El juego es muy simple pero muy nítido visualmente. A pesar de la lluvia de balas que te tiren, puedes identificar muy fácilmente el patrón de las balas y dónde se encuentra tu hurtbox.

[h3]Cosas Mejorables[/h3]

- [u][b]Música[/b][/u]: no es mala, pero es muy simple sinceramente y a veces hasta repetitiva. Creo que hay pocos soundtracks y se repiten bastante... si juegas dos o tres runs completas en el día terminarás con el cerebro medio taladrado de las mismas tonadas que tampoco es que estén muy inspiradas.

- [u][b]Variedad de niveles[/b][/u]: el juego tiene 6 niveles y 5 bosses y medio... es una pena que no haya alguna manera de variar tu recorrido, o que haya bosses distintos para enfrentar... en este aspecto, se hace un poco aburrido volver a sacar el 1cc con otra nave distinta pero sin variar en absoludo el recorrido de tu run. 

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

Por el precio que tiene y su propuesta directa y amena, es un juego muy recomendable.
No innova en nada, pero te da el entretenimiento y lijera variedad que esperas de un juego de este estilo.
Lo he disfrutado mucho y espero poder sacarle el 1cc con varias naves mas.

Game is pretty fun for what it is. But only get it on sale like I did for $1 (it was 90% off). It's not worth for the full price because it's very short. I beat it in an hour, there are only 6 short levels.

And other than the campaign mode, it has a boss rush mode and an endless mode where you fight generic repetitive non-boss enemies.

The last boss is extremely hard on normal. I don't play that many games of this type, but I'd say I probably played the best in the genre (Tyrian, Hydorah, Jamestown) and I'm pretty good at video games.
I played it on normal mode and I only died twice besides the deaths on the last level.
Right before I was going to rage quit and uninstall the game after many deaths (I wasn't willing to go through the whole campaign again on easy mode just to beat the final boss), I noticed that the slow down mechanic is permanent after you restart the fight on the final boss (maybe it's like that every time you die, I'm not sure) and you can deactivate it by activating the slow down thing yourself.
Playing with the permanent slow down thing on the final boss made it too easy, not playing it with the slow down thing made it too hard.

The game has many playable characters, but there's not that much opportunity to test that many because of how short the game is. Also, I feel like some are objectively better than others.

The chiptune music is really cool, but I wish it had more variety. All the songs kinda sound the same.

The story is generic, but it's ok for this type of game.

I can't help but think it would have been much better if it was 3 times the length.
Although get it for 1 buck like I did if you like shoot em ups.

Overall, a super fun game, even if there isn't too much to it. There's a surprising number of playable characters, 13 to be exact, but only 6 stages and 3 gamemodes (Arcade, the "story mode", Endless, and Boss Rush). These aren't super deep, but they don't need to be. It's a cheap and fun Shoot-Em-Up with plenty of fun content. Highly recommend this.

Il n'est pas avare en style de gameplay, possède des modes de jeu, de difficulté et selon moi est une bonne porte d'entrée à ceux qui veulent s'éssayer au genre!
Car le jeu a parfois certe des allure de danmaku, mais donne tout d'meme 2 atout majeurs aux joueurs: 
- Une barre de vie (que l'ont peut régénérer avec des bonus et qui selon le vaisseau est plus ou moin résistante)
- Et une barre de bullet time 

car oui, il vous sera possible de consommé une barre de bullet time à votre convenance dans les moment qui vous sembleront les plus propice.
Et meme si en soit le bullet time est pas très très "smooth"... pour pas dire qu'il fasse ramé le jeu (surtout quand des tremblement surviennent au meme moment), c'est de toute manière une feature dont ont peut se passé avec de la pratique.
Ainsi votre vaisseau aura sa barre de super tir en plus de son armement principal, qui évoluera en puissance avec 2 bonus distinct, un pour la puissance pure et l'autre pour plus de tir à l'écran.
Et le truc plutot cool avec ça, c'est que les innombrable petite babioles que vous ramassé pour une fois ne vous servirons pas seulement qu'au score, mais également à remplir à la fois vos jauge de super et de bullet time.

Ainsi, meme si avoir une barre de vie et plutot confort (surtout cotès fluidité de jeu, ne pas etre interrompue apres un hit cest cool) vous aurez tout dmeme le malus de laissé tombé quelques amélioration, que vous devrez reprendre ensuite et autant vous dire que parfois dans le feu nourri de l'action il peut etre assez facile tout faire capoté une partie qui semblé très bien mené.
Outre tout ça, pour je ne sais trop quel raison, vous aurez souvent du mal a ramassé les bonus, j'ai meme eu l'impression parfois de passé au traver d'eux, leur hitbox parait très bugué, mais c'est a peu près le seul réel défaut que j'aurais à reproché au jeu, je le recommande sans trop de mal .w .

Don't let the silly name put you off - this game is a seriously fun little shmup that has a lot more going for it than it's simple visuals and bullet hell leanings suggest at first glance.

Super Galaxy Squadron Ex Turbo is a bullet hell style shmup from the indie stable that looks at first glance to be "another one of those" - just a shmup made with a shooter-creator toolset with simple sprites and nice colours to look like it might have come out on a fictitious successor to the PC engine. From the videos and screenshots it looks like the dev has fallen into the usual trap of putting more bullets in it to make stuff harder and that you might find a couple of hours fun here only if you like bullet hell. I'm here to say that it definitely ISN'T any of those things and what SGS EX Turbo REALLY is needs you to buy it, experience it and realise that what you have here is a game that manages to walk that line of being able to teach good bullet hell fundamentals to players not normally tempted by the genre. 

I'm not a fan of bullet hell but I am acquiring an appreciation for it. Games like DoDonPachi Resurrection are a touch hard for me but games like Danmaku unlimited 3, Rolling Gunner and Crimzon Clover all scratch an itch in me that's tough to reach with my beloved Gradius, R-Type or Aleste. SGS Ex Turbo scratches the itch in a way that Danmaku unlimited 3 does while layering in a little R-Type like strategy with it's ship selection mechanics. If you are looking for variety in your indie bullet hell, this game has you covered as all the ships play sufficiently differently from one another that you'll find yourself staring to prefer certain ships for certain levels even after only a few plays. With 17 ships unlocked from the start, you won't need to be grinding score or resources like R-type Final 2 or Danmaku Unlimited 3 to get those extra loadouts - SGS Ex Turbo wants you to play with it's toys right out of the gate and even offers you the chance to switch ships at the beginning of every mission to let you swap out from a ship that may not suit your style or pick up a ship that may be better adapted to the challenges of the next level.

Following the theme of playing with all the toys, each ship has a primary and secondary shot that both fire from the one button. These weapons can be powered up by picking up items in the stage up to 5 times. Being hit de-powers your weapons by a rank by dropping some of your pickups, but you can reacquire lost pickups if you are quick. 
In addition to your main and secondary shots, each ship has access to a slow-down mechanic, allowing you to slow the game for short periods of time, helping you to survive the onslaught of bullets you may have to face. Lastly, each ship has it's own hyper weapon, activatable after you've filled an energy bar by picking up items left behind by defeated enemies. These hyper weapons are hugely variable between ships and often, these weapons shield your ship or cancel bullets in some way, allowing them to be deployed defensively as well as offensively.

The twin systems of the slow-down and hyper  weapons make SGS Ex Turbo quite forgiving to beginners. It's surprising how far you can get with just those systems but the game goes further in trying to ensure even the greenest of bullet-hell novices can come and play in the sandbox. The game has multiple difficulty modes and in some modes, your ship has a life bar that can be refilled with frequently occurring pickups throughout the level. Each ship has a different amount of damage it can take before a life is lost. Getting hit grants temporary invincibility, allowing players to brute force their way through patterns of bullets if they haven't yet acquired the skill, or the firepower, needed to get through. Additionally, your hit box is generously small, allowing unskilled players to marvel at how they managed to dodge through those impossible gaps, building confidence all the while.

When you add the simplicity of the powerup system, the additional tools the game gives players and the various game modes on offer, you really do get a game that can be a very effective introduction into bullet hell shooters. if you have ever looked at a bullet hell and wondered, "could I play that?" rest assured that SGS Ex Turbo will hold your hand a little and let you find your feet in an engaging and fun way......then it will tempt you to turn up the heat and feel like a badass. As a beginner, you'll have completed the game on the easier modes before you are 2 hours in and will be well on your way to high-score glory before you know it. Does this mean there's little for veterans of the genre to do here? Not at all - SGS Ex Turbo scales it's difficulty well and the higher skill-ceiling ships are a blast to get to grips with. I'll be playing this one for a while yet. 

I'd love to say that SGS Ex Turbo is flawless but, alas, there's a few nitpicks that bother me specifically. The graphical style isn't for me and it almost put me off buying. In play the style works great, however, and enemy bullets are always clear. The slow-down effect is somewhat jarring - it's like someone is pressing the pause button on autofire rather than like a true slowing mechanic, like in Ginga Force. The game doesn't really teach you some of the cool mechanics around certain ships (Black, White and Chrome come to mind) which have additional shooting modes or effects, typically used by not holding down your fire button. Lastly, on later difficulties it's very easy to get chain-hit in the dense patterns losing lives and power-ups rapidly one after the other. While this seems to be as the dev intends, i'm not a fan of being punished repeatedly for a single maneuvering mistake, particularly as my mobility issues sometimes make fine motor skills a little tough in a play session. Lastly, the appearance of the massive HYPER READY prompt annoyed me as it was a distraction - I'd have been happier with a simple tone or a Crimzon Clover-esque prompt underneath my ship as a reminder that my hyper is ready to go. 

These nitpicks are just that - nitpicks. None of them stop the game from being fun, they just wear the sheen off an otherwise fabulous little game for me specifically.

Before I go I have to mention the secret sauce that makes SGS Ex Turbo come together - the audio design. This game's explosions are meatier than they have any right to be and the soundtrack is memorable. i'll say this though - you NEED to finish the game because the end credits theme SLAPS. What a lovely way for the dev to reward a playthrough. Other indie devs take note - get a good composer in and have them design a theme that carries throughout, it will elevate your game. Just because you've chosen retro-style it doesn't mean your audio should be simple. THIS is how it's done with style!

Overall, SGS Ex Turbo is well worth your time, whatever skill level you are at. For £8.50 it's worth the price of entry but right now it's only £2.12 - that's an absolute steal for something with this much variety and fun. Don't miss this - it's a good one!

[h1]Summary[/h1]
Fun retro style pixel art vertical SHMUP with a large number of playable ships spanning various story stages and an optional endless mode and boss rush. Caution: The music will be stuck in your brain for years to come.

[h1]Who is it for?[/h1]

People who love crunchy pixel art and audio, retro STG/SHMUP fans in the market for something a little easier than the standard bullet hell and caravan shooters, people who dig this art style, people who like to try different ships and specials.

[h1]Who is it probably not for?[/h1]

People who want truly punishing bullet hell of the typical sort, people who dislike the pixel art, people who want more of a sense of progression or unlocks, people who like more complex mechanical interactions in their SHMUPS (e.g. Darius, R-Type, etc. - this is a very straightforward game with few moving parts for you to control,) people who want a super long game with dozens or hundreds of stages.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3118164898


[h1]PROS:[/h1]

[list]
[*]Accessible relative to most "bullet hell" shooters
[*]Still tough on harder difficulties
[*]Subjective, but for me this has some of the most satisfying audio and pixel art I've seen in a SHMUP - everything just hits my brain precisely the right way
[*]Voice acted story mode dialogue
[*]Boss rush mode
[*]Endless mode - every SHMUP should have this, it's so fun
[*]Tons of playable ships with distinct playstyles and specials
[*]Super catchy music that remains stuck in my head years after I first played
[*]The loop of collecting drops, entering focus to survive a little longer, firing a screen-wiping special, and then returning to the normal flow of play, is addictive in its simplicity and incredibly gratifying
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]

[list]
[*]Some may find six levels to be a tad brief
[*]Some may find it [i]too[/i] easy (but there are difficulty options even for the most hardcore imo, and 1CC-ing will still be a tough challenge... It just never quite rises to the level of super hardcore bullet hells some more experienced players may crave)
[/list]

[h1]Review[/h1]

Of all the retro style throwback SHMUPs made to date, I think this one is probably my favorite. It doesn't seek to be R-Type or Darius where you need to keep up with juggling multiple objects or abilities. It doesn't try to be the hardest bullet hell on the block or compete with vintage arcade STGs in that sense.

It's just an extremely easy to pick up and play (by genre standards at least, your personal mileage may vary of course) vertical SHMUP with a ton of personality and fun packed into it. Between that, its catchy music, and pleasantly granular pixel art, it feels more like a classic console SHMUP in many respects than a hardcore arcade shooter.

There's a story mode that spans six or so levels, with full voice acting. You have seventeen unique playable ships to choose from (the gelatinous donut called "Magenta" being my personal favorite,) each of which has its own speed, toughness, damage output, attack style, etc. Experiment to find your preference.

Controls couldn't be simpler. One button fires, another enters focus mode (in which you slow down, bullet-time style temporarily,) and another launches whatever your chosen ship's screen clearing special attack happens to be. Bank enough energy and keep your combo meter up, and you can enter hyper mode which if sustained nets you tons of damage and score.

Enemies drop energy (which is banked for specials and focus mode,) and attack upgrades. You aren't doing any loadout tinkering between stages ala Jets'n'Guns or the like. It's very simple. You're just picking powerups up and immediately getting the benefits on the fly, ala many of the classics. You lose them when you take damage, forcing you to try to pick them back up before they vanish.

Animations and hit registration feedback feel incredibly visually satisfying to me. Coupled with the sound design, attacks and explosions feel very visceral in that brain-pleasing way a lot of 90's games did. This game, I feel at least, nails that better than the vast majority of retro-inspired scrolling shooters on the market.

Bosses will require you to learn patterns, use focus mode to carefully dodge projectiles (though, again, not quite to the same high precision degree that hardcore bullet hells do, even though it clearly draws from those sorts of screen-filling flower-bloom-esque attacks for inspiration,) and survive long enough to destroy various hard points.

There's a boss rush mode and - my personal favorite - an endless mode in which you take on increasingly difficult waves of enemies, ultimately culminating with perpetual mini-bosses spamming the entire screen as you scramble in and out of focus mode to survive just long enough to take down each successive onslaught. There's no leaderboard, but you can screenshot your scores.

I'm not great by any means, and play pretty casually, but it's super satisfying all the same. This was my best score to date (again, Magenta is love, Magenta is life):

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3118228045

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

This is just a fun, nostalgic, genuinely satisfying blast to play. Definitely a sweet spot between difficulty and enjoyability in my opinion. If you're looking for something a little on the lighter side of the SHMUP world, you could do a lot worse. It feels like a real labor of love by its creators as well, which is always a joy to feel emanating from of a game while playing it.

After 20+ hours, an overly long attempt at a veteran Hardcore 1cc, as well as since dipping into several other Shmups and coming back, when asked if I would recommend this Game I'd have to (tentatively) say: No. 

I could write an entire essay but to keep it short - The simple fact is there are a lot of other Shmups that do everything better than SGS does for it to basically not be worth recommending over any of them - especially if it's going to potentially be your first Shmup (as it was mine). There's a lack of basic features such as save states and training modes, the level design is bland, and the core mechanics feel similarly lacking and I don't think it equips beginners with a decent enough grasp on either the fundamentals or potentials of the genre. 

There's so much more to say but I'll leave it at this. Shmups seem like short throwaway Games, but they aren't. To get the most out of them requires a lot of dedication. To earn that dedication from the Player, the Game needs to be as worthy in all of its aspects for a Player to really invest - and as it stands SGS just isn't good enough to earn that dedication... at least from me.

[b]Disclaimer: I have finished the EX Turbo version on the casual and veteran difficulties, and went through a single level (not beaten) in hardcore hell difficulty to measure stuff. As for the original game, I have finished it on normal mode.[/b]
Super Galaxy Squadron is a shmup game published by the very unlikely fellows at New Blood Interactive. And I mean it in a good way, as New Blood is not widely known as a publisher that releases shmups and you would think them releasing one would be an out of season April Fools joke.
One thing that most people often fail to mention is that by buying this game, you get two games: "Super Galaxy Squadron" which is the original game, and "Super Galaxy Squadron EX Turbo" which is the remake. You can select either of the games upon startup, and I'm going to look at both of them.

[h2]The Original[/h2]
This is the very first version of the game, released in 2015.  It gives you the option to try an endless experience, or play through the normal arcade experience on two difficulty modes: Normal mode which gives you an admittedly generous health system to work with, allowing you to heal using health pickups and also by grazing enemy bullets, and Hardcore mode which is literally the 1 hit death mode, where 1 mistake throws you back to the beginning of the level.
The initial impressions of the game are quite positive. The controls are responsive, the audiovisual presentation is solid, the explosions are punchy and feel good, there are quite a lot of playable ships to choose...  But the game gets repetitive and dull after a while, because of how the gameplay feels as a whole.

The thing is, the difficulty scales in an uneven manner throughout the game, due to enemy patterns not having a cohesive design and planning to them and feeling like they just appear randomly to make the game easier or harder. If you have played a decent number of shmups, you won't have much trouble disposing of normal enemy waves on any difficulty setting. However, there are times that the game suddenly increases the difficulty by bringing in multiple enemies that have complex bullet patterns, then goes back to its normal behavior after you dispose of them.
And this applies to the bosses as well. Bosses always have a significant difficulty increase compared to the enemies that came before them. They hit very hard as not only their bullet patterns are much faster and arrive in larger numbers compared to normal enemies, but also the brief invulnerability frames sometimes cannot keep you safe from the barrage of bullets, allowing you to get hit multiple times in advance. 

Another aspect of the gameplay that I absolutely hate in shmup games (and even talked about it in my Drainus review), is the weapons powering down after getting hit. When hit by enemy projectiles, your primary and secondary weapons lose some of their collected level ups, with them appearing in the level as floating items, giving you a chance to collect them and get your firepower back. There are two problems with this.
First, the powerups usually cannot be collected as either the barrage of incoming bullets prevents you from doing so, or you'll find them getting thrown towards the enemies/bosses. Second, you can lose up to 3 level ups on each hit, meaning you can lose a whole lot of them if you are not careful or have trouble reading the playing area with how much ♥♥♥♥ is getting thrown around. This is such a harsh punishment for lesser experienced players and casuals in my opinion as it lengthens the already punishing bosses.

Then we have the issue of the game suddenly losing its charm at half-way point. After Stage 3, you have seen everything the game has to offer. From this point onwards, no new enemy will be introduced (aside from the bosses) and the music for levels 4 and 5 will be repeats from levels 1 and 2 respectively. This makes for repetitiveness and dullness, soon to be replaced with misery as you approach the final boss.
Final Weapon is probably one of the most infuriating final bosses I had to face in a shmup game. This boss, contrary to all of the other bosses in the game, does not have any HP bar; so you'll never know how close you were to victory. The visual clutter shows its worst form in this boss fight as well, which forced me to stop following the boss around and divert my focus to a small area at the bottom of the screen and try to survive the encounter. Overall, it's not a fun boss to end the game with.

As I ended my 1cc playthrough in normal mode, the game managed to give me one final "♥♥♥♥ you" alongside one mini heart attack in the form of a fatal error. Thanks, I guess.
Now, it's time to get to the remake. Oh, and not the EX version as it's unavailable right now and therefore I know nothing about it. We're going straight to EX Turbo.

[h2]EX Turbo Super Ultra Championship Arcade Edition +R: Type [nu-bld] & Knuckles - Featuring Dante From The Devil May Cry Series[/h2]
Super Galaxy Squadron EX Turbo is the remake of the original game in a new Game Maker engine version which enhances a lot of stuff and adds a whole bunch of new features.
As obvious from the screenshots on the store page, the game has gotten a major overhaul in the presentation department. Graphically, the game looks much more high quality and cleaner. The redesigned user interface now makes use of the sides of the screen (which are completely empty in the original) and transfers all of the necessary information there in an easily identifiable manner. It even reacts to specific gameplay situations, providing visual cues whenever the overdrive mode gets activated or if the health is critically low, which is a much welcome addition for the player. The game now also shows each ship's attack style as well, which was a very good decision from the developers to make. Although it doesn't give you any visual information about their hyper attacks.
Storytelling has also been revamped. All story intermissions from the original game are now replaced with fully voice acted and animated cutscenes that have really good quality. Although there are no subtitles available. There are a bunch of gameplay additions as well. EX Turbo adds new difficulty options, a new boss rush mode, increases the score multiplier cap from 5 to 10, adds the new Overdrive and Focus (bullet time) abilities, adds a new boss (Harrier Ray), allows for ship switching at the beginning of every level, and nerfs the final boss to make it more tolerable while also giving them a HP bar.

Despite all these changes however, the core gameplay remains largely untouched. Enemy patterns still feel aimless, the difficulty spikes up and down occasionally in the manner explained before, there's no new music tracks or enemies, and the game still misses some crucial settings such as key rebinding. The only significant changes are the modifications to the final boss that make it somewhat more tolerable, and the addition of focus ability which gives you the power to slow down the bullets and dodge more efficiently.
But this ability is not without issues either. Upon using the new focus ability, the game turns into a jittery mess, because the game slows the frame rate down as well. The moment you press the focus button, the game goes from smooth 60 fps to jittery 30 fps, instead of just slowing down the gameplay speed.

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
Definitely not for everyone, and especially hardcore players, as the gameplay doesn't have much to write home about and feels very repetitive after a while. There are better alternatives to choose from.
